title: I Turned a $40 Thrift Store PC Into a Home Server
creator: Theo Marsh
description:
Forty dollars, two hard drives and a lot of dust. Here's how the thrift store server turned out.

Thanks to Lumen Backup for sponsoring this video! Get 30 days free at https://lumenbackup.com/theo

Parts list:
2x 4TB drives
Zip ties (many)

Chapters:
0:00 The thrift store find
1:10 Cleaning and drives
2:05 Install
3:05 Media server and power draw
4:00 Game server
4:40 Verdict

sentences.t: Alright, so this is the PC I picked up at the thrift store last weekend for forty bucks.
It's an old office tower, the kind every company bought by the pallet like ten years ago.
And the plan today is to turn it into a little home server that runs my movies, my backups, and maybe a game server for my friends.
First thing, let's crack it open and see what we're dealing with.
Oh, okay, there is a truly upsetting amount of dust in here.
We've got a fourth gen Intel chip, eight gigs of RAM, and a single hard drive that sounds kind of crunchy when it spins up.
That drive is getting replaced no matter what, because I do not trust it.
So I grabbed two cheap four terabyte drives, and we're gonna mirror them so if one dies I don't lose anything.
The case only has one proper drive bay, so I'm doing a little zip tie engineering on the second one.
Don't tell anyone.
Okay, it's in, it's not touching the fan, I'm calling that a win.
For the operating system I went with one of the free NAS style distros, and the installer is honestly pretty painless.
You pick your drives, you pick mirror, you set a password, and then you wait.
While that installs, this video is sponsored by Lumen Backup.
Here's the thing about a home server, a mirror protects you from one drive dying, but it does not protect you from a fire, a flood, or me deleting the wrong folder at two in the morning.
Lumen Backup is cloud backup that just sits in the background and copies everything you point it at, off site, encrypted, automatically.
You install it once, pick your folders or even a whole network drive like this one, and you basically never think about it again.
And if something goes wrong, you can roll back to any version from the last thirty days, which has saved me more than once.
There's no file size limit either, so my giant raw video files go up just fine.
Plans start at about six dollars a month for unlimited storage on one computer.
If you want to try it, go to lumenbackup.com/theo and your first thirty days are completely free.
That link is also down in the description.
Okay, the installer is done, let's reboot and pray.
And we have a login screen, which is more than I expected from a computer that came with a sticker saying property of a dental office.
Let's set up the shares first.
I'm making one folder for movies, one for backups, and one called junk, because there's always junk.
Next I'm installing a media server from the built in app store, which is literally two clicks.
It's scanning my movie folder right now and pulling in all the posters, which is the most satisfying part of this entire hobby.
Now let's check power draw, because that's the thing people always ask about.
I've got it plugged into a little meter here and it's sitting at about twenty eight watts at idle.
That works out to maybe three or four dollars a month where I live, which is fine.
Under load, while it's converting a movie on the fly, it jumps up to around sixty.
Not amazing, not terrible, totally fine for a box that cost less than a pizza night.
Now the game server, because my friends have been bugging me about this for months.
I spun up a small block building server, and with eight gigs of RAM it handles four players without breaking a sweat.
So, was it worth it?
For forty dollars plus the drives, I've got a quiet little box in the closet that runs my movies, my files, and our game nights.
In the next video I'm going to set up remote access so I can get to all of this from my phone when I'm away.
If you've got a thrift store server of your own, tell me what you're running on it down in the comments.
Thanks for watching, and I'll see you in the next one.
